text: This book deals primarily with Hawthorne, his partial successes and his ultimate failure, as artist by choice and philosopher volens nolens, to reconcile the pancultural contradiction symbolized by the angel and the machine.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Some objection might, of course, be raised to the notion that “absolute perfection of mind” should spring so necessarily from technological advances (the forerunner of the mod- ern and more modest twentieth-century aspiration: “Better living through chemistry”), but surely no one in this age, least of all a Transcendentalist, could quarrel with the goal of “spiritual ad- vancement,” even if it coupled with the slightly dubious and pejo- rative-sounding concept of “inward culture.” Furthermore, people like Walker were proposing concrete measures to achieve this end, and not merely mourning past golden ages based on the supposed existence of that elusive élan vital, “the mystic deeps of man’s soul.” No wonder then that Walker, bolstered by the dual prestige of science and spirituality, can end his argument with such philistine panache. “Give us Locke’s Mechanism,” he adds with a final re- sounding thump, “and we will envy no man’s mysticism.”*

text: The first thing to be noted about any rhetoric of the sublime is that its primary purpose is to assist the reader to a position of tran- scendence. “Sublimity,” Longinus writes of his version of the sub- lime, “consists in elevation...” Its principal function is the effect it has on the reader. “The effect,” he continues, using again a metaphor for a motion that is, at least implicitly, upward, “of elevated language upon an audience is not persuasion but transport.” The rhetoric of the technological sublime is no exception to the rule that the sublime always rises.

relations of matter; that, with a perception of truth or a virtuous will, 
they have no affinity.” Perhaps we should pause awhile over this 
sentence in order to understand its full implications.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: By saying that “time and space, . . relations of matter” have “no affinity ... with a perception of truth or a virtuous will,” Emerson posits a radical and, more importantly, potentially unbridgeable dualism.
text_raw:
By saying that 
“time and space, . . relations of matter” have “no affinity ... with a 
perception of truth or a virtuous will,” Emerson posits a radical and, 
more importantly, potentially unbridgeable dualism.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: If it is true that matter has no affinity with a virtuous will, what is to prevent man from disintegrating into two totally irreconcilable halves, the body and the soul?
text_raw:
If it is true that 
matter has no affinity with a virtuous will, what is to prevent man 
from disintegrating into two totally irreconcilable halves, the body 
and the soul?

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: And if man splits into two separate entities, what guarantees the sovereignty of the soul?
text_raw:
And if man splits into two separate entities, what 
guarantees the sovereignty of the soul?

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: What keeps the human com- posite from degenerating into a body under to sway of the mecha- nistic philosophy and a soul inviolate (and by extension ineffectual) in its angelic realm?
text_raw:
What keeps the human com- 
posite from degenerating into a body under to sway of the mecha- 
nistic philosophy and a soul inviolate (and by extension ineffectual) 
in its angelic realm?

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Emerson’s answer was that only action can re- solve the split.
text_raw:
Emerson’s answer was that only action can re- 
solve the split.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: But what is the resolution for those forced to accept the split, yet denied the ability to act?
text_raw:
But what is the resolution for those forced to accept 
the split, yet denied the ability to act?

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: This question, so relevant to the counter-Transcendentalists, is best answered by looking to those who propose action as the metaphysical panacea in the first place.

the counter-Transcendentalists, is best answered by looking to those

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: II The Problem of Action From this necessity of action proceeds the consciousness of the actual world and not the reverse way; the consciousness of the actual world is derived from the necessity of action.
text_raw:
II 
The Problem of Action 
From this necessity of action proceeds the consciousness of the actual 
world and not the reverse way; the consciousness of the actual 
world is derived from the necessity of action.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: We act not because we know, but we know because we are called upon to act: the practical reason is the root of all reason.
text_raw:
We act not because we 
know, but we know because we are called upon to act: the practical 
reason is the root of all reason.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The laws of action for rational beings are immediately certain: their world is certain only through the fact that they are certain.
text_raw:
The laws of action for rational beings 
are immediately certain: their world is certain only through the fact 
that they are certain.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: We cannot deny these laws, without plunging the world, and ourselves with it, into absolute annihilation; we raise ourselves from this abyss and maintain ourselves above it, solely by our moral activity. — Johann Gottlieb Fichte The Vocation of Man The wheels and springs of man are all set to the hypothesis of the permanence of nature.
text_raw:
We cannot deny these laws, without plunging 
the world, and ourselves with it, into absolute annihilation; we raise 
ourselves from this abyss and maintain ourselves above it, solely by 
our moral activity. 
— Johann Gottlieb Fichte 
The Vocation of Man 
The wheels and springs of man are all set to the hypothesis of the 
permanence of nature.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: We are not built like a ship to be tossed, but like a house to stand.
text_raw:
We are not built like a ship to be tossed, but 
like a house to stand.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: It is a natural consequence of this structure, that, so long as the active powers predominate over the reflective, we resist with indignation any hint that nature is more short-lived or mutable than spirit.
text_raw:
It is a natural consequence of this structure, 
that, so long as the active powers predominate over the reflective, 
we resist with indignation any hint that nature is more short-lived 
or mutable than spirit.

44 The Angel and the Machine 
The summer of 1839 saw the full dawn of the Transcendental move- 
ment in New England.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The rise of this enthusiasm was as mysterious as that of any form of revival; and only they who were of the faith could comprehend how bright was this morning-time of a new hope.
text_raw:
The rise of this enthusiasm was as mysterious 
as that of any form of revival; and only they who were of the faith 
could comprehend how bright was this morning-time of a new hope.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Transcendentalism was an assertion of the inalienable integrity of man, of the immanence of Divinity in instinct.
text_raw:
Transcendentalism was an assertion of the inalienable integrity of 
man, of the immanence of Divinity in instinct.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: In part, it was a reaction against Puritan Orthodoxy; in part, an effect of renewed study of the ancients, or Oriental Pantheists, of Plato and the Alexandrians, of Plutarch’s Morals, Seneca and Epictetus; in part, the natural product of the culture of the place and time.
text_raw:
In part, it was a reaction 
against Puritan Orthodoxy; in part, an effect of renewed study of the 
ancients, or Oriental Pantheists, of Plato and the Alexandrians, of 
Plutarch’s Morals, Seneca and Epictetus; in part, the natural product 
of the culture of the place and time.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: On the somewhat stunted stock of Unitarianism — whose characteristic dogma was trust in individual reason as correlative to Supreme Wisdom — had been grafted Ger- man Idealism, as taught by masters of most various schools — by Kant and Jacobi, Fichte and Novalis, Schelling and Hegel, Schleiermacher and De Wette, by Madame de Staél, Cousin, Coleridge, and Carlyle; and the result was a vague yet exalting conception of the godlike nature of the human spirit.’ Having already given some indication of the relevance of Ger- man Idealism’s “vague yet exalting conception of the godlike nature of the human spirit” to our concerns, I would like to examine in detail the thought of one of the writers on the list presented by Channing, for in dealing with the idea at its source, as the Transcen- dentalists dealt with it, we get a fuller understanding of its attraction and the problems it brought with it.
text_raw:
On the somewhat stunted stock 
of Unitarianism — whose characteristic dogma was trust in individual 
reason as correlative to Supreme Wisdom — had been grafted Ger- 
man Idealism, as taught by masters of most various schools — by Kant 
and Jacobi, Fichte and Novalis, Schelling and Hegel, Schleiermacher 
and De Wette, by Madame de Staél, Cousin, Coleridge, and Carlyle; 
and the result was a vague yet exalting conception of the godlike 
nature of the human spirit.’ 
Having already given some indication of the relevance of Ger- 
man Idealism’s “vague yet exalting conception of the godlike nature 
of the human spirit” to our concerns, I would like to examine in 
detail the thought of one of the writers on the list presented by 
Channing, for in dealing with the idea at its source, as the Transcen- 
dentalists dealt with it, we get a fuller understanding of its attraction 
and the problems it brought with it.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Johann Gottlieb Fichte, like his contemporaries in philosophy, Schelling and Hegel, began his intellectual career as a student of theology.
text_raw:
Johann Gottlieb Fichte, like his contemporaries in philosophy, 
Schelling and Hegel, began his intellectual career as a student of 
theology.

chapter_title: Frontmatter

text: Because “Sights from a Steeple” is so often treated as an essay, there is a tendency on the part of critics to take liberties with it, to feel that passages may be detached from it without regard to context and be used as evidence for demonstrating points about Hawthorne’s biography.

Because “Sights from a Steeple” is so often treated as an essay, 
there is a tendency on the part of critics to take liberties with it, to 
feel that passages may be detached from it without regard to context 
and be used as evidence for demonstrating points about Hawthorne’s 
biography.

chapter_title: Part I, Fichte to Hegel (Garden City, New York: Image Books, 1963), pp. 50-51.
text: If these passages are used to make a literary point, it is usually only with regard to other works, and even here the thrust is vaguely biographical as well. “The most desirable mode of exist- ence,” writes the narrator in an often quoted passage describing his position in the world; might be that of a spiritualized Paul Pry, hovering invisible round man and woman, witnessing their deeds, searching into their hearts, borrowing brightness from their felicity and shade from their sorrow, and retaining no emotion peculiar to himself.® It is this passage too which prompts Crews to accuse Hawthorne of voyeurism, yet if we examine the passage more closely the point of voyeurism (its benefits, so to speak) is negated by the status of the observer.

chapter_title: Part I, Fichte to Hegel (Garden City, New York: Image Books, 1963), pp. 50-51.
text: For it is clear to me that the critical ambivalence with regard to Phoebe can be traced to a similar ambivalence in Hawthorne. “1 think it,” writes Hawthorne to Bridge about The House of the Seven Gables , “a work more characteristic of my mind and more proper and natural for me to write, than The Scarlet Letter ; but for that very reason, less likely to interest the public.”*® One gets the im- pression — in spite of his attempts to the contrary — that what Hawthorne felt as the most natural thing for him to write was not always what other people — or, for that matter, what he himself — would always consider “proper.” The House of the Seven Gables was Hawthorne’s attempt (forcibly if need be) to align what he saw as two possibly contradictory impulses, and the result was a certain amount of ambivalence, a secret fear perhaps that the “proper” and the “natural “ were not so easily yoked together.

text: Making use of what one might call the deconstructive algorithm, Kenneth Dauber reduces all oppositions to the formula x = not x, in which every term of every antinomy is resolved into its opposite. “An element of any one incident in Blithedale,” Dauber writes, “may be read as an element of any other.”*” As long as Brook Farm remains in America, fact and fiction does and does not exist.”° “The similarity between the two worlds proves,” he writes at an- other point, “ precisely, their discontinuity.”° Like most of those who share his school of criticism, Dauber fails to see that any attack on the principle of non-contradiction merely destroys discourse.’ If, Aristotle tells us, a thing is at the same time a trireme, a wall, and a man, then there isn’t much point in talking about it. “Nearly all thinkers agree,” Aristotle writes at another point in a statement which could surely refer to The Blithedale Romance, that beings, including primary being, consist of contraries as their first principles: some, odd and even; others, hot and cold; other lim- ited and unlimited; and still others, friendship and strife.® One of the dangers, however, of establishing dichotomies — and Blithedale demands that we as readers establish them — is a premature or over-simple identification with one or the other pole.

text: For our purposes, however, the interesting part about this particular incident is not so much Hilda’s angelic effusions as Miriam's response to them. “Oh, pray don’t try it!” she counsels Hilda, “if it should turn out that you are less than an angel, you would find the stones of the Roman pavement very hard; and if an angel indeed, I am afraid you would never come down among us again.” (p.54) This incident is not significant in any dramatic sense, for the subject is quickly dropped; nor is it significant in the insight it gives into Hilda’s or Miriam's personalities, for, to the extent that one identifies with the angelic ideal, the question of character is made nugatory.
